lesson_title: Measure a Cliff Without Leaving the Beach
hook_text: The boat never moved. The cliff was never climbed. One angle gave away the whole distance.
clip_script: From the top of a vertical cliff 30 metres high, the angle of depression to a boat is 25 degrees. How far out is the boat? Here is the trick that unlocks it: the level line at the cliff top and the sea below are parallel, so the 25 degrees looking down equals the 25 degrees the boat sees looking up — alternate angles, guaranteed. Now the triangle at the boat's corner: the cliff is the opposite side, 30 metres; the distance to the base is the adjacent — that pair belongs to tangent. Tan 25 degrees equals 30 over d, so d equals 30 divided by tan 25 degrees — 64,3 metres. No boat ride, no measuring tape across the water. One angle, one ratio, and the sea gives up its secret.
visual_style: Golden-hour drone shot of a cliff and a fishing boat, a glowing level line snapping across the cliff top, the equal angles pulsing at top and boat, then the triangle drawing itself over the scene with 30 m and 64,3 m labels counting up.
pacing: Slow reveal of the parallel lines, sharp beat on 'alternate angles', brisk run through the tangent step, hold on the final distance.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn any story into a triangle.
